notes.shape: The yield curve plots Treasury yields across maturities from 1 month to 30 years, with a normal upward slope indicating higher yields for longer maturities due to risk and time preferences. An inverted yield curve, where short-term yields exceed long-term yields, has historically preceded US recessions by 6-18 months. Currently, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.61% (due June 2026), and the 10-year to 2-year spread is positive at 0.45 percentage points. This marks a shift from the 2022-2024 period when the curve was inverted with the spread below zero, representing the deepest inversion recorded at 0.0 points in this series.
notes.signal: The 2-year to 10-year spread (2s10s) functions as a key recession indicator, with inversion historically signaling increased recession risks. The spread was inverted throughout 2022-2024 but has since 're-steepened' above zero to 0.45 points, reflecting a recent normalization in yield differentials. However, the yield curve often un-inverts shortly before the onset of a recession, tempering straightforward interpretations. Complementing this, the NY Fed's recession probability stands at 31%, suggesting a moderate but not extreme risk of recession based on current data.
notes.now: The current upward slope of the yield curve, as evidenced by a positive 0.45 point 2s10s spread and a 10-year yield of 4.61%, indicates a reduced immediate signal of recession compared to the recent inversion period. Nonetheless, the 31% probability from the NY Fed highlights that recession risks remain materially present. Overall, the curve suggests a cautiously improving economic outlook without negating the possibility of future downturns.
